$$
{y}^{″}=3y+4{e}^{2x},\,y(0)=-2,\,{y}^{′}(0)=0.

feedback.problem:
Use the Taylor series method to find a series solution about $x=0$, in ascending powers of $x$ up to and including the term in ${x}^{3},$  of the initial value problem

$$
{y}^{″}=2y-6\operatorname{cos}⁡x,\,y(0)=-2,\,{y}^{′}(0)=2.
$$
feedback.worked_solution:
We wish to express $y(x)$ as a Taylor series about $x=0$:

$$
y(x)=y(0)+x{y}^{′}(0)+\frac{{x}^{2}}{2!}{y}^{″}(0)+\frac{{x}^{3}}{3!}{y}^{(3)}(0)+⋯
$$

We're given $y(0)$ and ${y}^{′}(0),$ so we need to calculate ${y}^{″}(0)$ and ${y}^{(3)}(0).$

We know that $y(0)=-2,$ so we substitute this into the given equation to find ${y}^{″}(0):$

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{″}(0) & =2y(0)-6\operatorname{cos}⁡0 \\  & =2(-2)-6(1) \\  & =-10\end{aligned}
$$

Next, to find an expression for ${y}^{(3)}(x),$ we differentiate both sides on the given equation with respect to $x:$ 

$$
{y}^{(3)}=2{y}^{′}+6\operatorname{sin}⁡(x)
$$

We can now find  ${y}^{(3)}(0)$ by substituting in the known values:

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{(3)}(0) & =2{y}^{′}(0)+6\operatorname{sin}⁡(0) \\  & =2(2)+0 \\  & =4\end{aligned}
$$

Finaly, we  substitute  the obtained values in  the Taylor series:

$$
\begin{aligned}y(x) & =y(0)+x{y}^{′}(0)+\frac{{x}^{2}}{2!}{y}^{″}(0)+\frac{{x}^{3}}{3!}{y}^{(3)}(0)+⋯ \\ y(x) & =-2+x\cdot 2+\frac{{x}^{2}}{2!}\cdot (-10)+\frac{{x}^{3}}{3!}\cdot 4+⋯ \\ y(x) & =-2+2x-5{x}^{2}+\frac{2{x}^{3}}{3}⋯\end{aligned}
$$
